business_problem: Amsterdam City Archives needed to make a massive paper archive usable for the public despite handwritten documents, outdated Dutch, and limited search tools that made discovery difficult.
solution_summary: Amsterdam City Archives, Capgemini, and Microsoft built Chat with History as an agentic AI research assistant over centuries of archival material. The archive first prepared an AI-ready data layer by digitizing documents and applying Transkribus plus handwritten character recognition to transcribe hard-to-read records. Capgemini and Microsoft then used Azure AI Foundry, AI Search, Microsoft Agent Framework, and Speech Services Avatar to create a secure multilingual chatbot that translates old Dutch into modern Dutch, interprets archival material, and answers natural-language questions in the user’s language. Rather than just returning search hits, the system connects and contextualizes source material so users can ask questions such as when a street was built or how children played in the seventeenth century. The result shifts the archive from a passive document repository to an interactive knowledge service that makes cultural heritage searchable and explorable for a global audience.

solution_components.name: AI Search

solution_components.name: Microsoft Agent Framework

solution_components.name: Speech Services Avatar
solution_components.role: Supports richer conversational interaction within the history experience.

data_flow: Archival documents are digitized and transcribed with Transkribus and handwritten character recognition, indexed through AI Search, interpreted in Azure AI Foundry with agentic AI, and then delivered through Chat with History so users can ask natural-language questions and receive contextualized answers.

Potential future use of old maps and photos
business_outcome: Amsterdam City Archives turned a hard-to-navigate paper archive into a multilingual conversational knowledge service, improving public access to cultural heritage and establishing a reusable model for archive digitization and discovery.
metrics: By the end of 2025, about two percent of the archive will be digitized
